title: Dental plaque & the oral biofilm
blurb: What plaque really is, how it hardens into calculus, where calculus builds up and why it keeps gum disease going.
question: At a check-up the dentist points out hard, creamy-yellow deposits on the tongue side of a patient's lower front teeth, and dark, gritty deposits just under the gum on some molars. The patient says, "But I brush every day." What are these deposits, why do they collect in those places, and why won't brushing shift them?

teach.body: Dental plaque is a soft, sticky film of bacteria living in a gel-like matrix they make themselves. It is a biofilm: an organised community stuck to the tooth, not loose food debris. Plaque is pale and hard to see until it builds up, which is why we use disclosing tablets or solution to stain it for patients. It cannot be rinsed away with water or mouthwash. It has to be physically disrupted by brushing and interdental cleaning, every day.

teach.h: How plaque builds up after cleaning

steps.label: Pellicle forms
steps.sub: A thin protein film from saliva coats the clean tooth within minutes

steps.label: Early colonisers stick
steps.sub: Mainly streptococci attach to the pellicle within hours

steps.label: Biofilm matures
steps.sub: More species join over days; deep layers become low in oxygen (anaerobic)

teach.caption: Brushing resets the clock. The longer plaque is left, the more harmful its bacteria become, and eventually it hardens.

children.label: Caries
children.sub: Bacteria make acid that dissolves enamel

teach.caption: Plaque is the primary cause of both caries and periodontal disease (gingivitis and periodontitis).

teach.h: Calculus: plaque that has turned hard
teach.body: Calculus (tartar) is mineralised plaque. Calcium and phosphate salts from saliva, or from the fluid that seeps out of the gum crevice, are deposited into undisturbed plaque until it sets hard. Calculus itself does not cause disease directly, but it is always coated in a fresh layer of living plaque, and its rough surface holds even more. That makes it a plaque-retentive factor. It is firmly stuck on, so brushing cannot remove it: it needs scaling by a dentist, hygienist or therapist.

rows.label: Position
values: Below the gum, in the pocket

teach.caption: Subgingival calculus is dark because it takes up pigment from blood in the inflamed pocket. It is often seen once gums recede.

Heaviest on the LINGUAL of the lower incisors and canines (near the submandibular and sublingual duct openings under the tongue) and the BUCCAL of the upper molars (opposite the parotid duct opening). Saliva pools there, rich in calcium and phosphate.
Thick creamy-yellow calculus on the lower front teeth, with red, swollen gums bleeding at the margins. Plaque and calculus left in place keep the gums inflamed.

teach.note: Anything that makes plaque harder to remove raises the risk of caries and gum disease. Scaling and correcting overhangs are part of periodontal care.

teach.text: Plaque and calculus are not the same thing. Plaque is SOFT and comes off with a toothbrush and interdental cleaning. Calculus is HARD, mineralised plaque that only professional scaling removes. Rinsing alone removes neither.

items: Plaque is a bacterial biofilm on the acquired pellicle; it is the primary cause of caries and gum disease.
It must be removed mechanically every day; disclosing agents make it visible.
Calculus is mineralised plaque: supragingival (yellow, from saliva) or subgingival (dark, from crevice fluid).
Calculus collects most on the lingual of lower incisors and buccal of upper molars.
Calculus, overhangs, crowding and appliances are plaque-retentive factors.

summary: You can now explain that plaque is a bacterial biofilm and the root cause of caries and gum disease, describe how it hardens into supragingival and subgingival calculus, say where calculus builds up and why, and list the plaque-retentive factors that make disease more likely.

A.q: A patient asks what dental plaque actually is. Which answer is most accurate?
options: A sticky bacterial biofilm on the teeth
Hardened mineral deposits stuck to enamel
A protein layer formed from saliva
A.why: Plaque is an organised community of bacteria in a sticky matrix, attached to the tooth surface: a biofilm.

whyNot.0: Food debris is loose and washes away; plaque is a structured bacterial film.
whyNot.2: Hardened mineral deposits describe calculus, which is mineralised plaque.
whyNot.3: The protein layer from saliva is the acquired pellicle, which plaque forms on.

A.q: While the dentist scales a patient's teeth, where would you expect the heaviest supragingival calculus to be?
A.why: The submandibular and sublingual ducts open under the tongue, so mineral-rich saliva bathes the lingual of the lower incisors.

whyNot.0: The upper molar buccal surfaces collect calculus (near the parotid duct), not typically the lower molar buccal.
whyNot.1: The palatal of the upper incisors is not near a major duct opening.
whyNot.3: Occlusal surfaces are cleaned by chewing and are a site for caries rather than calculus.

A.q: Which statement about calculus is correct?
options: It can be removed by careful brushing
It only forms below the gum margin
It is caused by eating too much sugar
A.why: Calculus forms when calcium phosphate salts are deposited into undisturbed plaque until it hardens.

whyNot.0: Calculus is firmly attached and needs professional scaling; brushing can't remove it.
whyNot.1: Calculus forms both above (supragingival) and below (subgingival) the gum margin.
whyNot.2: Sugar drives caries; calculus comes from minerals in saliva or crevice fluid.

B.q: On probing below the gum margin of a lower molar, the dentist finds hard, dark brown deposits on the root. What are they most likely to be?
B.why: Calculus below the gum margin is subgingival: dark from blood pigments, hard and firmly attached to the root.

whyNot.1: Supragingival calculus sits above the gum and is usually creamy white or yellow.
whyNot.2: Tobacco stain is a surface discolouration on visible tooth, not a hard deposit under the gum.
whyNot.3: Arrested caries is a hard lesion in the tooth itself, not a deposit stuck onto it.

B.q: Why is calculus described as a plaque-retentive factor?
options: It releases acid directly onto the gums
It stops saliva reaching the gum margin
Its rough surface holds more plaque
It blocks fluoride from reaching enamel
B.why: Calculus is always coated in living plaque, and its rough surface traps more, keeping bacteria against the gum.

whyNot.0: Calculus is mineral; it is the plaque on top of it that causes harm.
whyNot.1: Saliva still reaches the area; in fact saliva supplies the minerals for supragingival calculus.
whyNot.3: Retaining plaque is the problem; calculus is not described as a fluoride barrier.

B.q: Which of these is NOT a plaque-retentive factor?
B.why: A smooth, well-contoured restoration doesn't trap plaque. The others all create ledges or extra surfaces that do.

whyNot.0: An overhang leaves a ledge at the margin where plaque collects.
whyNot.2: Clasps and denture bases give plaque extra surfaces to cling to.
whyNot.3: Brackets and wires make cleaning harder and hold plaque around them.

C.q: Within minutes of a tooth being polished clean, what forms on its surface first?
C.why: Salivary proteins coat a clean tooth within minutes to form the acquired pellicle, which bacteria then stick to.

whyNot.0: Calculus only forms when plaque is left undisturbed long enough to mineralise.
whyNot.1: A mature, anaerobic biofilm takes days to develop.
whyNot.2: A white spot lesion is early caries from repeated acid attack, not a surface film.

C.q: A patient has heavy plaque, calculus and bleeding gums. Which behaviour has most likely contributed?
options: Brushing often with a soft brush
Poor plaque control at the gum line
C.why: Plaque left at the gum margin inflames the gums and mineralises into calculus.

whyNot.0: Frequent brushing with a soft brush helps remove plaque.
whyNot.1: Fluoride toothpaste protects against caries; it doesn't cause calculus or bleeding.
whyNot.3: Water with meals is harmless and helps clear food.

C.q: Why does supragingival calculus build up fastest on the lingual surfaces of the lower incisors?
options: The tongue presses plaque into that area
These teeth have the thinnest enamel
C.why: The submandibular and sublingual ducts open beneath the tongue, bathing these surfaces in calcium- and phosphate-rich saliva.

whyNot.1: The tongue tends to clean surfaces; it doesn't push plaque in.
whyNot.2: Enamel thickness has nothing to do with where calculus forms.
whyNot.3: Heavy brushing would remove plaque, not encourage calculus.

reteach.title: Slime in a vase, scale in a kettle
reteach.question: Think of the slime that coats a flower vase if it isn't scrubbed, and the hard scale inside a kettle. How do they map onto plaque and calculus?

blocks.body: Leave a vase of flowers and a slippery film grows on the glass. Rinsing doesn't shift it; you have to scrub. That is plaque: a living film that needs brushing and interdental cleaning. Now think of a kettle in a hard-water area. Minerals in the water slowly build into crusty scale that no sponge will remove. That is calculus: minerals from saliva turning old plaque to stone. And just like scale, it is rough, so more slime grows on it.

blocks.h: Plaque vs calculus at a glance
Calculus at the neck of the tooth
blocks.caption: Deposits sit at the gum margin, right where they keep the gingiva inflamed.

explain.h: Plaque: a biofilm you have to scrub
explain.body: Plaque forms on the acquired pellicle within hours of cleaning and matures over days. Because it is a sticky, organised biofilm, only mechanical cleaning (toothbrush plus interdental brushes or floss) breaks it up. Disclosing agents stain it so patients can see what they've missed.

test.q: What is the most effective way for a patient to remove dental plaque?
options: Rinsing well with water after meals
test.why: Plaque is a sticky biofilm, so it must be physically disrupted by brushing and cleaning between the teeth.

whyNot.0: Water rinses away loose debris but not an attached biofilm.
whyNot.2: Gum boosts saliva but doesn't remove established plaque.
whyNot.3: Mouthwash can't break up an established biofilm on its own.

explain.body: Calcium and phosphate are deposited into plaque that is left undisturbed. Above the gum the minerals come from saliva, giving creamy-yellow supragingival calculus. Below the gum they come from gingival crevicular fluid, giving dark, hard subgingival calculus.

test.q: Where do the minerals in subgingival calculus mainly come from?
test.why: Below the gum margin, minerals come from the fluid that seeps out of the gum crevice (gingival crevicular fluid).

whyNot.0: Saliva supplies the minerals for supragingival calculus, above the gum.
whyNot.1: Calculus forms on cementum; it isn't made from it.
whyNot.2: Dietary calcium isn't deposited directly into plaque.

explain.body: Calculus builds up where saliva pools near the major duct openings: the lingual of the lower incisors (submandibular and sublingual ducts) and the buccal of the upper molars (parotid duct). Expect to see these sites need most scaling.

test.q: In the upper arch, which surfaces usually collect the most supragingival calculus?
test.why: The parotid duct opens opposite the upper second molar, so the buccal surfaces of the upper molars collect calculus.

whyNot.1: The upper palatal incisor surfaces are not near a major duct opening.
whyNot.2: Occlusal surfaces are scrubbed by chewing.
whyNot.3: Labial canine surfaces are easy to brush and away from duct openings.

explain.body: Anything that holds plaque against the teeth raises disease risk: calculus, overhanging or poorly shaped restorations, crowding, appliances and dentures. Poor plaque control and irregular attendance let deposits build up unchecked.

explain.caption: Dark deposits at the gum margins of several lower front teeth, with red, swollen gums bleeding around the incisors.

test.q: During charting the dentist notes an overhanging filling on 46. Why does this matter for the gums?
options: It traps plaque at the margin
It releases mercury into the gum
It makes the tooth more sensitive
It stops the tooth from erupting
test.why: An overhang leaves a ledge that collects plaque and is hard to clean, inflaming the gum next to it.

whyNot.1: Set amalgam does not leak mercury into the gum in any clinically meaningful way.
whyNot.2: Overhangs affect the gum and plaque control, not tooth sensitivity.
whyNot.3: 46 is an erupted adult tooth; overhangs don't affect eruption.
